title: Elements: A River Worth Returning To

finalObjectives.text: Place the floating lantern at the gathering landing.

ending: The table is laid, the atlas is finished, and a lantern floats at our landing. From four beginnings, a river full of things to share. Come and sit with us.
limits: Author-aware structural replay only. Not source-blind playtesting, browser/UI verification, historical or scientific re-verification, or evidence of fun.

steps.message: Clay. Soft, fine earth that holds an impressed shape while wet.
Stone. Hard, rough mineral material; its weight and abrasive surfaces can do work.
Bowl. An open, hollow vessel with a broad mouth and a stable base.

Brick. A hard, regular block of fired clay, made for stacking into lasting structures. A bowl to eat from and bricks to build with—not bad for four beginnings. Now we need something worth putting in that bowl.
Our next stop: The first supper. We’re taking what we need with us; the things we leave stay here. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Rain. Water arriving from the sky, enough to soak the ground rather than fill a vessel neatly.
Plant. A living stem with roots and leaves; a source of several different natural materials.
Grain. Dry edible seeds with a tough outer surface and a starchy interior.
Flour. Fine meal ground from grain. Loose and powdery until it is wetted.
Dough. A soft mass of flour and water. It can hold its shape, but has not yet risen or baked.
Flatbread. A simple cooked bread without a raised, airy crumb.
Fruit. Ripe, juicy produce with flesh around its seeds.

Fruit juice. The fruit's liquid, separated from its flesh; sweet enough to feed fermentation. Flatbread and juice: a proper first supper. Take your time; we can look for somewhere to rest before the next stretch of river.
Our next stop: A place to wake up. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Wood. Rough timber: solid lengths with grain and bulk, not flat boards yet.
House. A small weatherproof home with solid walls and a timber roof. Its dark interior would benefit from a fitted window.
Sand. Small, hard mineral grains. Loose when poured, abrasive when rubbed.
Glass. A hard, clear material that lets light through but needs shaping to give it a particular job.
Window. A pane held in a wooden frame, admitting light while closing an opening.
Window fitted to House.
Plant fiber. Loose strands from plant stems. Flexible, but not yet organized into a strong length or sheet.
Thread. A long, fine strand spun from fibers; useful for binding and stitching.
Cloth. A flexible sheet made from interlaced threads.

Sleeping mat. A padded woven surface that separates a sleeper from the cold ground. Daylight through the window, and a mat for the night: thank you, the cottage feels like a home now. The brook is just beyond the orchard.
Our next stop: Across the brook. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Axe. A sharp stone edge on a handle. Its job is to cut and shape wood, not to pound it.
Planks. Flat, cut boards with broad faces and straight edges; easier to join into surfaces than rough timber.
Rope. Thicker cordage that can hold a load or keep larger pieces together.
Footbridge. A narrow deck spanning the brook, supported and held together above the water.
Wheel. A solid wooden disc, shaped to roll or turn around its centre. Its rim is still smooth.
Wheelset. Wheels mounted on a wooden axle: a rolling undercarriage, not yet a load-carrying body.
Handcart. A small rolling platform for moving a load by hand.
Paper pulp. Wet, separated plant fibers suspended in water.
Paper. A thin, dry sheet of joined fibers; a surface for marks and records.

Crossing map. A portable record of the brook crossing, so the bridge itself can stay where it belongs. A bridge for our feet, a cart for our loads, and a map for the next traveller. Downstream, the miller has been watching that same water go to waste.
Our next stop: The mill bend. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Waterwheel. A paddled wheel that moving water can turn. Its turning force still needs a connection to useful work.
Wooden gear. A wooden wheel with teeth cut around its rim, able to pass rotation to another mechanism.
Mill gearing. A connected drive taking rotation from the waterwheel toward the grinding machinery.
Millstone. A heavy circular grinding stone. It can crush grain, but will not turn by itself.
Grain mill. A water-driven grinding machine built for the village's daily grain, not just a single handful.
Sack. A stitched cloth bag, closed at the sides and open at the top.

Flour sack. A sack filled with flour, ready to take to the baker. You could grind a handful before; now the village has a mill to do the work. Take that flour sack to the baker—she has a lighter loaf in mind.
Our next stop: Bread for the journey. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Wild starter. A living flour culture. Given moisture and time, it makes gas and changes dough.
Placed.
Risen dough. Dough expanded by fermentation, with small bubbles held inside it.
Bread. A baked loaf with an airy crumb and a firm crust.
Basket. A light woven carrier with enough shape to hold its contents together.

Picnic basket. A basket packed with bread for a journey. There it is: a loaf with air in its crumb, and a basket for the road. The orchard keeper has been wondering how to save a little summer for the gathering.
Our next stop: Keep the summer. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Jam. Fruit cooked down into a thick spread; it still needs a vessel for keeping.
Jar. A hollow clay container with a narrower opening than a bowl.
Preserve jar. A jar filled with fruit preserve, but not yet covered.
Jar lid. A fitted wooden cover for the mouth of a jar.
Sealed preserves. Fruit preserve put away in a covered jar for later meals.
Cider. A fermented fruit drink, no longer the fresh juice it began as.
Glaze. A mineral coating for pottery; its finished surface depends on the potter's firing.
Glazed bottle. A narrow-necked ceramic vessel with a finished, glazed surface.

Cider bottle. A closed vessel of cider, ready to carry without spilling. Preserves under a lid and cider in a bottle. We can bring something of this orchard to the gathering without asking the fruit to stay ripe forever.
Our next stop: The potters yard. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Placed.
Glazed bowl. A fired bowl with a smooth, finished surface rather than bare porous clay.
Table. A sturdy raised wooden surface for preparing, displaying or serving things.
Tile. A flat, regular piece of shaped clay for covering a surface.

Tiled table. A table with a durable tiled top, easy to wipe after a shared meal. A smooth bowl and a table made for many suppers. Useful things can be beautiful, too. Our neighbours at the quarry could use a little of your ingenuity.
Our next stop: Tools to lend. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Hammerstone. A blunt cobble for striking, rather than a cutting edge.
Iron ore. Rock containing iron-bearing minerals, not usable metal yet.
Kiln. An enclosed firing chamber that concentrates heat around pottery or other materials.
Bellows. A flexible air chamber that pushes a directed flow into a fire.
Forge. A hot working hearth with a forced air supply for metalworking.
Iron. Workable metal: strong enough for edges, fasteners and fittings once shaped.
Pickaxe. A pointed metal head on a handle, suited to breaking hard ground and rock.
Nails. Pointed metal fasteners; their stems can also serve as small pins.
Wooden chest. A box assembled from boards, with room to protect things inside.
Hinge. Metal leaves joined around a pin can swing while remaining connected.

Tool chest. A wooden chest with a hinged lid, keeping shared tools together. A pickaxe for hard ground and a chest to keep our tools together. Leave them within reach of the next pair of hands; there is wider water ahead.
Our next stop: A river wide enough. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Pier post. A stout prepared post, ready to support a landing above the water.
Dock. A fixed landing where a boat can meet the shore.
Raft. Timbers bound into a floating platform, without a sail.
Sail. A broad sheet rigged to catch the wind and pull on its lines.
Sailboat. A small floating craft able to use the wind for movement.

River map. A record linking the crossing and boat landing along the river. A landing, a sailboat, and another stretch added to the map. The river is beginning to join our villages instead of keeping them apart.
Our next stop: A light to come home to. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Tower. A tall masonry structure with an opening to look out from above its surroundings.
Charcoal. A dark, carbon-rich material made from wood under controlled firing.
Torch. A hand-held source of flame and light on a wooden support.
Lantern. A light protected by a clear enclosure rather than left as an exposed flame.
Placed.
Lighthouse. A high harbour light that can be seen from the water.
Float. A buoyant, sealed object that stays on the water's surface.
Mooring buoy. A floating marker with a line to hold a boat in place.

Harbour map. The river map extended to include the harbour's light and approach. A light above the water, a buoy below it, and a harbour marked on the map. Now let us think about the people those boats will bring.
Our next stop: The walled garden. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Seeds. Small beginnings for new plants, gathered from mature growth.
Seedlings. Young growing plants, still tender and in need of support or shelter.
Trellis. An open framework of stretched lines, giving climbing stems something to grip.
Climbing garden. Young plants trained up a trellis rather than left to trail on the ground.

Greenhouse. A light-filled shelter protecting tender plants from the weather. The climbing plants have support, and the tender ones have shelter. We have made them a good beginning; those uphill beds still need water.
Our next stop: Water without the climb. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Carving tool. A sharpened metal cutting tool for careful shaping rather than broad chopping.
Saw. A toothed metal edge for cutting wood along a controlled line.
Hollow pipe. A wooden conduit with an open passage through its length.
Water channel. A supported waterway directing flow along a planned route.
Reservoir. A lined storage basin, ready to hold a supply of water.
Pump. A mechanism for lifting or moving water; its moving parts still need power.
Water pump. A pump coupled to a waterwheel, using the stream's motion to lift water.
Filled reservoir. A storage basin supplied by the pump rather than carried buckets.
Irrigation channel. A channel connected to the stored water supply.
Irrigated garden. The climbing garden with water delivered to its beds. Water reaches the garden without another climb with a bucket. That leaves more hands free to prepare a welcome for our guests.
Our next stop: A welcome in colour. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Loom. A frame that holds threads under tension so they can be woven in order.
Flowers. The colourful blossoms of a living plant.
Dye. Colour extracted into a liquid, able to stain absorbent material.
Dyed cloth. Cloth that has taken up colour through its fibers.
Patterned cloth. Woven cloth with a deliberate arrangement of colours.
Festival banner. A patterned flag on a support, visible above the crowd.
Awning. Cloth stretched over a supporting frame to give shade.
Canopy. A supported and tied covering sheltering a larger open space. A banner to find us by and a canopy to gather beneath—it looks like a welcome. Now we ought to send the invitation.
Our next stop: News before the boats. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Ink. Dark liquid pigment that leaves a readable mark on a light surface.
Letter. A written message that can travel separately from its author.
Mailboat. A boat carrying written messages between settlements.
Printing block. A wooden face carved with a design that can be repeated.
Inked printing block. A printing face coated with ink on its raised surfaces.

Printed invitations. Repeated printed notices inviting people to the river gathering. The invitations are printed and the mailboat is ready. We have something to tell our neighbours—and soon we will need something for them to hear.
Our next stop: A tune in the square. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Hollow tube. A small wooden tube with an open interior, ready to carry air or hold aligned parts.
Flute. A hollow wind instrument whose vibrating air makes a note.
Drum. A stretched surface over a hollow body, resonating when struck.
Platform. A flat, supported deck raised above the ground.

Bandstand. A sheltered raised place where musicians can gather and be heard. A flute, a drum, and a place for the players. That is the beginning of a fine gathering. Leave a little room for the storyteller.
Our next stop: A story to pass on. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Curtain. Hanging cloth that can cover or reveal an opening.
Stage. A raised performance space with a curtain to reveal the action.
Puppet. A small figure made to be moved while telling a story.
Puppet theatre. A little performance stage built around moving figures and their stories.
Bound book. A stack of pages held together along one edge, ready to preserve a sequence.
Paint. A prepared coloured medium that can cover a surface with visible shapes.
Picture. A deliberately painted image, not merely a blank sheet or a pot of colour.

Picture book. A bound sequence of images that can tell a story after the storyteller leaves. A little theatre for moving stories, and a picture book for keeping them. There are other stories nearby, too—even in a drop from the pond.
Our next stop: What the water hides. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Lens. A shaped, polished piece of glass that bends light.
Magnifier. A lens held in a frame for examining nearby small details.
Telescope. Lenses aligned in a tube for viewing things that are far away.
Microscope. An arrangement of magnifying optics for seeing very small nearby details.
Pond water. A collected drop from the still pond, with more in it than the eye first sees.
Glass slide. A small flat piece of clear glass that can support a thin sample.

Pond slide. A thin pond-water sample supported on clear glass for close examination. A pond sample and the means to look closely. We need not travel far to find something unfamiliar; let us look at the plants along this same river.
Our next stop: Names for the green world. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Leaf study. An observed account of a leaf's small structures, seen through a lens.
Botanical drawing. A recorded plant study showing the features an observer noticed.
Pressed plant specimen. A flattened, preserved plant sample retaining its visible form.
Herbarium. A bound collection of preserved plant specimens with room for their records.

Illustrated flora. A guide joining preserved specimens to drawings of their distinguishing features. Specimens and drawings, together in a flora we can share. A traveller can compare a leaf with the page instead of relying on our memories.
Our next stop: A promise to the sky. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Windsock. A light fabric tube that turns and extends with the wind.
Measuring jar. A vessel with a marked scale, making amounts comparable rather than guessed.
Rain gauge. A marked collector showing how much rain has fallen.
Rain record. Written measurements from repeated readings of the rain gauge.

Weather record. An account bringing rainfall and wind observations together. We have a record of wind and rain, not just a guess at the sky. I will keep it with our preparations; the shore cook is planning the crossing meals.
Our next stop: Food for the crossing. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Smoke. The airborne products of a smouldering wood fire, not the heat alone.
Net. An open mesh that can let water through while catching larger things.
Fish. A catch brought from the shore, still in need of preparation for keeping.
Smoked fish. Fish prepared with smoke for the journey; represented here without a real preservation procedure.
Vinegar. A sharp, acidic liquid made as a fermented drink changes in contact with air.
Pickles. Fruit preserved in an acidic liquid rather than eaten fresh.
Pickle jar. A container holding the prepared pickles for transport. Smoked fish and a jar of pickles: provisions for a boat without a hearth. The guests on shore will need looking after as well.
Our next stop: Water for everyone. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Washstand. A basin held at a comfortable height for washing.
Filter bed. Layers of granular material that can catch some suspended matter from water.
Water filter. A filter bed held in a conduit so water can pass through it.
Filtered water. Water after passing through the filter; clearer does not automatically mean safe.
Boiled water. Water that has been heated to boiling; this is not a promise to remove every contaminant.
Drinking-water bowl. A serving bowl of the water prepared for this fictional gathering.
Covered urn. A large ceramic vessel with a fitted cover, protecting what is put inside.

Drinking-water urn. The gathering's prepared water in a covered serving vessel. The washstand and covered water urn are ready. A welcome is more than decoration; it is noticing what people will need when they arrive.
Our next stop: The cellar before winter. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Grain bin. A substantial wooden store for dry grain.
Drying rack. An open frame and mesh allowing air to reach food from several sides.
Dried fruit. Fruit from which much of the moisture has been removed.
Crock. A thick-walled clay storage vessel, sturdier than the small jar.
Sealed crock. A storage crock fitted with its cover.
Fruit crock. A covered crock holding dried fruit for later meals. Room for grain, and dried fruit put away in its crock. We can celebrate the season without forgetting the one that follows it.
Our next stop: Lights on the water. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Paper lantern frame. A light wooden framework covered in paper, awaiting its source of light.
Seed oil. Liquid pressed from seeds, able to carry energy and feed a wick.
Wick. Absorbent fibers carrying oil toward a flame.
Oil lamp. A small vessel holding oil and a wick for a steady light.
Paper lantern. A small light enclosed in a paper-covered frame.
Floating lantern. A lantern supported upright on a buoyant base.

Watch lamp. An oil light protected by glass for the night watch. A light that can float and a lamp for the watch. Keep the floating lantern for our sheltered landing; first, let us agree when everyone should arrive.
Our next stop: When the boats arrive. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Pendulum. A suspended weight that swings back and forth with a regular rhythm.
Clockwork. A powered, regulated train of moving parts; much more than a freely spinning wheel.
Clock. A housed timekeeping mechanism with a readable indication of time.
Ferry timetable. A timetable records departure times against stops on the river.
Bell. A hollow metal body shaped to ring when struck.

Dinner bell. A bell hung with a pull line, ready to call people together. A timetable for the boats and a bell to call us together. The last visitors will come after dark; the watcher has been studying their route.
Our next stop: Above the headland. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Star chart. A drawn record of the stars' positions, used to recognize the sky.
Tripod. A three-legged support that holds an instrument steadily above the ground.
Mounted telescope. A telescope on a stable stand, keeping the view steady.

Navigation chart. A route record joined to the night sky, for someone who has not made this journey before. River landmarks and stars on one navigation chart, with a steady telescope beside it. We can leave the next traveller something better than vague directions.
Our next stop: A roof for the pictures. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Arch. A curved masonry span carrying weight around an opening.
Arcade. A covered walkway built around an open masonry span.
Gallery. A sheltered public space displaying pictures for people to see together.
Exhibition catalogue. A portable record of the images displayed in the gallery.
Mosaic pieces. Small pieces of coloured glass prepared to be arranged into an image.

Mosaic. An image assembled from small pieces held in a clay bed. A mosaic on display and a catalogue to carry away. Our gathering has things to look at as well as things to eat; the kitchen is nearly ready for us.
Our next stop: Before the great cooking. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Ash. The mineral residue left after a fire has consumed its fuel.
Lye. An alkaline material associated with wood ash; hazardous outside this simplified story.
Soap. A washing material formed from fats or oils and alkali; no real making procedure is provided here.
Wash station. A washstand supplied with soap for the people preparing the meal. Soap at the washstand, where the cooks can use it. Now we can turn from preparing the kitchen to preparing the meal.
Our next stop: A kitchen for the crowd. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Stove. An enclosed cooking structure with a durable metal heating surface.
Cooking pot. A heat-resistant vessel with a broad opening for stirring food as it cooks.
Placed.
Porridge. Grain cooked into a warm, soft meal.
Placed.

Fruit compote. Fruit softened by cooking into a spoonable dish. The stove is ready, with porridge and fruit compote for the early arrivals. Bring the gathering to the table; we have been preparing for this together.
Our next stop: A river worth returning to. Bring the useful things; leave the rest where we made them. We collect the things needed for this scene along the way.
Feast. Bread and fruit prepared as a meal to share.
Feast table. The communal table laid with food, ready for guests.
Weather book. A bound record preserving the season's observations of wind and rain.
River atlas. A durable account of the route and its changing weather, left for future travellers.
Placed. The table is laid, the atlas is finished, and a lantern floats at our landing. From four beginnings, a river full of things to share. Come and sit with us.
